title: The new wine (Luke 5:27–39)
hook: Levi's big feast, and no one after drinking old wine wants new

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hole in a roof and a man who took up his bed. Your line was we have seen strange things today. Did you help someone get where they needed to go? Day five hundred twenty-one.

A tax booth on a road near the lake. Levi sits behind it, collecting customs on goods passing through. It's steady money, and it does not make him popular. Earlier in Luke, John the Baptist tells tax collectors to collect no more than they're owed, which says something about their reputation. Jesus walks up and says two words: "Follow me." And Luke says, "he left all, rose up, and followed him." No negotiation. No two weeks' notice. Then Levi does what people do when their life changes overnight. He throws a party. A big one, in his own house. And he invites everyone he knows, which, for a tax collector, means a lot of other tax collectors.

Some Pharisees and their scribes watch the feast and ask the disciples: "Why do ye eat and drink with publicans and sinners?" For them, who you ate with mattered; a shared table was a sign of belonging, and they took holiness seriously. Jesus answers: "They that are whole need not a physician; but they that are sick. I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance." Then they ask about fasting: John's disciples fast, yours eat and drink. And Jesus answers with pictures from the kitchen. Nobody tears a patch from a new coat to fix an old one. Nobody pours new wine into old wineskins: "else the new wine will burst the bottles, and be spilled." Bottles here are wineskins, leather bags. New wine is still fermenting, still giving off gas and stretching. An old skin, already stretched and stiff, can't give anymore, and it splits. "But new wine must be put into new bottles; and both are preserved." Something new needs room to grow. And then a last line, and it's almost a joke: "No man also having drunk old wine straightway desireth new: for he saith, The old is better." Jesus knows people. We like what we know. New wine tastes rough at first. Readers have heard this many ways: some as gentle patience with people slow to change, others as a wry smile at how hard change is. Either way, it's honest. Levi changed overnight. Others take longer. The text seems to make room for both.
screen: then, large: `NEW WINE MUST BE PUT INTO NEW BOTTLES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: try a new habit gently. Settle, and breathe. Think of something new you've wanted to start: a few minutes of quiet in the morning, a walk, reading, calling someone more often, going to bed earlier. If part of you says the old way is fine, notice it. That's not a villain; it's just old wine talking. Now, instead of a big plan, picture the smallest new skin you could make room for. One minute instead of thirty. One evening a week, not every night. Something that can stretch as it grows. Imagine doing it today, gently, without forcing it. If you pray, you can ask for patience with your own pace. If you don't, simply let the small new thing feel welcome. The bell holds the time.
Wineskins. The leather bags Jesus says new wine needs: old ones, already stretched stiff, split; new ones give the wine room to grow.
Your line: new wine takes time. Do your tiny new thing today, and if part of you still prefers the old, smile at it and do the new thing anyway. Day five hundred twenty-one.

howItsDone: Christians remember Levi as Matthew, the tax collector who became an apostle, and many churches read the call of Levi as a picture of welcome at the table.

fork.setup: you're Levi. a teacher walks up to your tax booth and says: follow me. what do you do?
options: leave everything, get up, and follow, then throw a feast.
fork.reveal: Levi leaves all and follows, then throws a great feast in his own house for everyone he knows.

original.note: Greek: a wineskin, a leather bag. the "bottles" of the King James Bible.

trapdoor: what you thought: new wine, old bottles, a saying about change.
what it means: something new and alive needs room to grow, and Jesus admits that people who love the old rarely want the new straight away.
what a scholar hears: the "bottles" are askoi, leather wineskins; an old one has already stretched as far as it will go.
recall: Latin for magnify, the song's first word

notes: Pharisees framed fairly (table fellowship and holiness taken seriously). Keeper to confirm tone.
Textual variant in 5:39: chrestoteros ('better', Textus Receptus) vs chrestos ('good', critical texts). Confirm.
Levi identified with Matthew (Matthew 9:9) in howItsDone as Christian tradition.
Tax collectors described generally ('often took more than they should'); avoid overstating.
